query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In Q235 steel’s pre‐exposure state, the corrosion resistance in harsh chloride environments is governed by the integrity of its naturally formed oxide layer. When exposed at an elevated temperature, the enhanced metal diffusion is predicted to promote the repair and densification of the native oxide film, thereby suppressing localized corrosion compared to the room temperature condition.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its as‐received condition with its naturally formed native oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Expose identical Q235 steel coupons to a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution under controlled laboratory conditions at room temperature (~25°C) and at an elevated temperature (~80°C).
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted using identical immersion durations (e.g., 100 hours), constant NaCl concentration, controlled pH, oxygenation, and agitation to simulate harsh chloride-rich environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The continuity, density, and integrity of the native oxide film on the steel surface.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperature, increased thermal energy enhances metal ion diffusion, which facilitates the formation of a more continuous, dense, and adherent oxide film. In contrast, at room temperature the limited diffusivity yields a more porous, defective oxide that offers inferior protection against localized corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to specimens maintained at room temperature, those exposed at the elevated temperature are predicted to develop a more uniform and protective oxide layer, exhibit lower corrosion current densities in electrochemical tests, and show reduced localized corrosion features.
generation.baseline: Q235 steel exposed to the same corrosive (chloride‐rich) environment at room temperature (~25°C) with its native oxide layer intact.
generation.boundary: This predicted behavior is anticipated under moderate temperature elevation (around 80°C) in chloride-rich conditions; under extreme temperatures or with substantially different environmental chemistries, other corrosion mechanisms may become dominant.
generation.uncertainty: Although enhanced diffusivity at elevated temperatures is expected to improve oxide integrity, competing effects such as thermal stress-induced cracking might counteract these benefits. Further investigation is needed to determine which effect prevails.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of Q235 steel coupons with their native oxide intact and divide them into two groups. Immerse one group in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution maintained at room temperature (~25°C) and the other in the same solution maintained at an elevated temperature (~80°C) for the same duration (e.g., 100 hours). After exposure, use surface analytical techniques and electrochemical measurements to assess oxide film morphology and quantify corrosion performance.
measurements: SEM imaging to evaluate the continuity and any cracking of the oxide film
EDS/XPS analyses to assess the composition and density of the oxide layer
Tafel polarization and EIS to determine corrosion current densities and impedance characteristics
Gravimetric analysis to measure mass loss due to corrosion
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the elevated temperature specimens do not exhibit a significantly more continuous, dense oxide film and do not show notably reduced corrosion current densities and mass losses compared to the room temperature specimens, then the hypothesis—that enhanced temperature-induced diffusion improves oxide protection and suppresses corrosion—will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this paper, CrMnFeCoNi HEA coatings with different ZrC contents were prepared on Q235 steel by a PTA process, and the effects of ZrC on the morphology, composition, hardness, friction, and corrosion properties of the coatings were investigated.

cited_evidence.kind: web:Thermal stability and applicability to nuclear applications
cited_evidence.text: The use of HEAs in nuclear applications depends greatly on their microstructural stability in the extreme environments of the operating conditions. Although Cr18Mn27Fe27.5Ni27.5 alloy shows good mechanical properties and relatively high resistance to radiation damage, this study showed that the alloy experienced phase instability at 700 °C after 1000 hours. Cr-rich particles were found to precipitate in the alloy, even well beneath the corrosion affected region, after the high temperature exposure during the corrosion test. Just underneath the surface, few fine circular Cr-rich precipitates were observed. As the distance from the surface increased, the Cr-rich precipitates’ concentration increased and their morphology became more needle-shaped as shown in Fig. 6. Then, the precipitates’ concentration decreased significantly but persisted through the entire thickness of the sample as shown in Figs. 6 and 9. These changes in the concentration and morphology of the Cr-rich precipitates indicate that the precipitation process not only depends on both the annealing temperature and duration, but also on the Mn concentration in the alloy, which varies due to its dissolution in the salt.

In this paper, the CoCrFeNiTix HEA coatings are prepared on Q235 steel substrate by laser cladding. The effect of Ti content on the microstructure and corrosion resistance in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution was studied. Furthermore, the corrosion resistance mechanism was analyzed experimentally and by first-principles calculations.

drafts.hypothesis: The native iron oxide layer present on pre-exposed Q235 steel acts as a protective passivation barrier in room temperature harsh environments, but at elevated temperatures thermal stress causes this layer to crack, exposing fresh metal and thus accelerating localized corrosion.
drafts.material_initial_state: Untreated Q235 carbon steel with its naturally formed native oxide scale.
drafts.intervention: Comparison of samples with the native oxide layer intact versus samples where the oxide layer has been carefully removed (e.g., via polishing).
drafts.conditions: Exposure to a chloride-containing corrosive solution (e.g., 3.5% NaCl) under controlled room temperature (~25°C) and elevated temperature (~80°C) conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: The integrity and microstructural coherence of the native oxide layer mediate the shift from corrosion suppression to corrosion initiation.
drafts.mechanism: At room temperature, the intact native oxide acts as a coherent, protective barrier that limits ionic penetration and inhibits corrosion. However, at elevated temperatures, mismatches in thermal expansion induce microcracking in the oxide film, leading to localized breakdown of passivation, exposure of the underlying metal, and the onset of pitting corrosion driven by aggressive chloride ions.
drafts.predicted_outcome: At room temperature, samples with the native oxide layer intact will exhibit lower corrosion rates and a more uniform surface compared to polished samples without the oxide. In contrast, at elevated temperatures, the intact oxide samples will show increased localized corrosion (e.g., higher pit density and deeper pits) relative to the polished samples, where a more uniformly reformed oxide layer may develop.
drafts.baseline: Untreated Q235 steel with its native oxide layer exposed to the same conditions.
drafts.boundary: Findings are expected for Q235 steel with typical composition and pre-exposure oxide characteristics in static, chloride-rich environments; results may vary with differences in environmental dynamics or surface preparation methods.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of Q235 samples: one group retains the native oxide layer, and a second group is polished to remove the oxide. Both groups are then exposed to a 3.5% NaCl solution at 25°C and at 80°C for equivalent durations. Post-exposure, use surface microscopy (SEM), electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), and gravimetric analysis to assess corrosion behavior.
measurements: Pit density and depth via SEM
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy data (indicative of barrier properties)
Surface microstructural changes and oxide integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis would be falsified if (a) at room temperature, the oxide-intact samples do not show lower corrosion rates or more uniform corrosion behavior compared to polished samples, or (b) at elevated temperatures, the oxide-intact samples fail to exhibit a statistically significant increase in localized corrosion (e.g., pit formation) relative to the polished samples.

drafts.hypothesis: The pre-existing, naturally formed thin oxide layer on Q235 steel initially suppresses corrosion by serving as a passivating barrier at room temperature; however, at elevated temperatures, thermal stresses compromise the oxide layer’s integrity (through cracking or spallation), which then accelerates corrosion-related degradation.
drafts.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state with its native, naturally formed thin oxide layer.
drafts.intervention: Deliberate alteration of the surface oxide: one set retains the natural oxide, a second set undergoes a controlled thermal oxidation to enhance and thicken the oxide layer, and a third set has the oxide mechanically removed.
drafts.conditions: Exposure to a harsh corrosive environment (e.g., 3.5% NaCl solution) under controlled laboratory conditions at room temperature (approximately 25°C) and at an elevated temperature (approximately 80°C) for fixed durations.
drafts.structural_mediator: The continuity and integrity of the oxide layer present on the steel surface.
drafts.mechanism: At room temperature, the intact oxide layer acts as a barrier to oxygen and aggressive ions, thereby reducing corrosion onset. When exposed to elevated temperatures, mismatch in thermal expansion between the oxide and the steel substrate induces cracking or spallation in the oxide layer, allowing corrosive species to penetrate the steel and initiate localized corrosion.
drafts.predicted_outcome: At room temperature, the samples with an intact or enhanced oxide layer are expected to display lower corrosion rates compared to samples with the oxide removed. At elevated temperatures, the oxide-enhanced samples are predicted to exhibit an accelerated corrosion rate relative to the untreated natural oxide samples due to thermal destabilization and cracking, while the oxide-removed samples are likely to corrode fastest overall.
drafts.baseline: Q235 steel with its naturally formed oxide layer under room temperature conditions in a 3.5% NaCl solution.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is presumed valid for Q235 steel and similar carbon steels in chloride-rich environments where temperature is the dominant variable; variations in steel composition or alternative aggressive media might influence the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of Q235 steel samples: (1) with the natural oxide layer intact, (2) with an enhanced oxide layer via controlled thermal oxidation, and (3) with the oxide layer mechanically removed. Expose the samples to a 3.5% NaCl solution at both room temperature (approx. 25°C) and elevated temperature (approx. 80°C) for a defined duration. Use electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to monitor the corrosion rate dynamically, and utilize scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to assess surface oxide integrity and morphology post-exposure.
measurements: Corrosion rate determined by EIS (e.g., charge-transfer resistance)
Qualitative and quantitative SEM imaging of oxide layer morphology and evidence of cracking or spallation
Comparison of pit initiation and growth features among the three sample sets
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the enhanced oxide samples do not exhibit a reduction in corrosion at room temperature relative to the natural oxide samples, or if no increased corrosion degradation (as indicated by EIS and SEM) is observed in the enhanced oxide samples at elevated temperatures compared to the natural oxide samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In unexposed Q235 steel, the kinetics of native iron oxide film formation govern the onset or suppression of corrosion in harsh chloride environments: at elevated temperatures, faster diffusion promotes the rapid development of a dense, adherent oxide layer that acts as a barrier to further degradation, whereas at room temperature the slower oxide formation yields a more porous, defective film that accelerates localized corrosion.
drafts.material_initial_state: Q235 carbon steel in its pre-exposure state with its native, thin oxide film and uniform microstructure
drafts.intervention: Expose identical Q235 steel coupons to a chloride-rich environment (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution) under controlled aerated conditions at room temperature and at a moderately elevated temperature (e.g., ~70°C)
drafts.conditions: Controlled immersion tests in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution, with one set maintained at room temperature (~25°C) and another at an elevated temperature (~70°C); oxygen availability and chloride concentration kept constant across tests
drafts.structural_mediator: The integrity, density, and continuity of the native Fe oxide film developing on the steel surface
drafts.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, enhanced atomic mobility accelerates the oxidation of iron, leading to the rapid formation of a continuous, adherent Fe oxide layer that temporarily suppresses further chloride-induced corrosion. In contrast, at room temperature, the slower diffusion rates result in a porous and discontinuous oxide film that fails to protect the underlying metal, thus favoring localized anodic dissolution and increased corrosion.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Specimens exposed at elevated temperatures will initially exhibit lower corrosion rates (e.g., lower corrosion current densities and mass losses) and demonstrate a thicker, more continuous oxide film (as revealed by SEM/XPS) compared to those tested at room temperature.
drafts.baseline: Q235 steel samples exposed to the identical chloride environment at room temperature serve as the untreated reference condition
drafts.boundary: This protective effect is expected to hold at moderate elevated temperatures where oxide film integrity is maintained; at excessively high temperatures, thermal stresses might induce cracking in the oxide layer, negating its protective role.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple sets of Q235 steel coupons with identical pre-exposure conditions. Immerse them in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution under controlled aerated conditions. Maintain one set at room temperature (~25°C) and another at an elevated temperature (~70°C). Periodically assess the corrosion behavior over a fixed time period using electrochemical techniques (e.g., EIS and potentiodynamic polarization) and mass loss measurements. Subsequently, conduct surface and cross-sectional microstructural characterizations (using SEM, XPS, and optical microscopy) to analyze the oxide film’s continuity, thickness, and protective quality.
measurements: Corrosion current density from potentiodynamic polarization
Polarization resistance and impedance spectra from EIS
Surface morphology and oxide film thickness via SEM and XPS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the elevated temperature specimens do not exhibit a lower corrosion rate (i.e., similar or higher corrosion current densities and mass loss) and do not develop a denser, more continuous oxide film compared to the room temperature specimens, then the proposed mechanism of temperature-enhanced protective oxide formation is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In Q235 steel’s pre‐exposure state, the onset (or suppression) of corrosion in harsh environments is governed by the differential ability of minor alloying elements (especially manganese) to migrate to the surface and form a protective, continuous oxide layer. At room temperature, slow Mn diffusion leads to a discontinuous or defect‐laden native oxide, which facilitates localized corrosion; whereas at moderately elevated temperatures, enhanced Mn diffusion enables the formation of a Mn‐rich mixed Fe–Mn oxide that is more adherent and protective, thereby suppressing further corrosion-related degradation.
drafts.material_initial_state: Q235 carbon steel with its as-received microstructure (characteristic low alloy carbon steel with typical trace Mn content) and naturally formed native oxide layer.
drafts.intervention: Expose Q235 specimens to an aggressive environment (e.g., a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution) under two controlled thermal conditions—room temperature (~25°C) and an elevated temperature (~80°C).
drafts.conditions: Identical exposure durations (e.g., 100 hours), same NaCl concentration, controlled pH and dissolved oxygen levels, and similar agitation conditions to simulate harsh, corrosive environments; testing performed at both room temperature and at a moderately elevated temperature where atomic diffusion is enhanced.
drafts.structural_mediator: The microstructural quality of the surface oxide and specifically the extent of manganese segregation at grain boundaries and the oxide–metal interface that enables formation of a continuous, dense, and protective mixed oxide.
drafts.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, thermal energy enhances the diffusion of Mn from the steel’s near-surface regions to the interface, leading to the formation of a Mn-enriched oxide film that acts as a barrier against corrosive attack. In contrast, at room temperature, the limited diffusion of Mn results in a thinner, less adherent, and possibly non-uniform native oxide that fails to prevent localized corrosion.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated Q235 steel maintained at room temperature, specimens exposed at elevated temperature will develop a more uniform and Mn-enriched oxide layer, exhibit lower corrosion current densities in polarization tests, and show a reduced rate of localized corrosion pits.
drafts.baseline: Untreated Q235 steel exposed to harsh environments at room temperature, which typically forms a defective native oxide layer and shows higher corrosion rates.
drafts.boundary: The effect is anticipated within moderate temperature elevations (up to around 80–100°C) in oxidizing, chloride-rich environments. Under extreme temperatures or drastically different chemistries, other mechanisms may dominate the corrosion behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of Q235 steel specimens and divide them into two groups. Immerse one group in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at room temperature (~25°C) and the other in the same solution maintained at an elevated temperature (~80°C) for an identical duration (e.g., 100 hours). After exposure, perform surface analyses (SEM, EDS, XPS) to assess oxide layer morphology and composition, particularly the Mn enrichment. In parallel, conduct electrochemical Tafel and polarization tests to quantify corrosion rates.
measurements: SEM imaging to assess oxide layer continuity and pit formation
EDS elemental mapping to quantify Mn (and Fe) concentrations in the oxide
XPS for detailed chemical state analysis of the oxide film
Electrochemical measurements (Tafel plots, corrosion current densities)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the elevated temperature specimens do not exhibit a significantly more continuous, Mn-rich (and hence more protective) oxide layer and do not have notably lower corrosion rates compared to the room temperature specimens, then the hypothesis that enhanced Mn diffusion at elevated temperatures is responsible for suppressing corrosion will be falsified.
